Replit's Nix and Agent infrastructure is one of the most extensively engineered but partially documented platforms in the developertools space. Below is the most comprehensive public synthesis available, drawing directly from Replit's engineering blog posts, opensource contributions, and technical disclosures. Where Replit has not publicly documented specific internals, that boundary is clearly marked.



 Part I — Replit's Nix Infrastructure

 Nix Evaluator Backend

Replit uses the standard upstream C++ Nix evaluator — not a custom reimplementation — to process replit.nix files. The evaluator is invoked through nix-shell, which evaluates the derivation expression and resolves all package closures into a set of /nix/store/ paths. There is no evidence Replit has written a custom Nix evaluator from scratch; their engineering work has focused instead on the caching layer that sits above the evaluator, and on the store architecture below it.[1]

The most significant performance innovation Replit made to the evaluation path is the environment variable cache, stored at .cache/replit/nix/env.json inside every REPL's filesystem. Prior to this optimization, every REPL startup triggered a full nix-shell evaluation of replit.nix, which could consume seconds to tens of seconds of wallclock time. The cached JSON file stores the entire set of environment variables that nix-shell would produce — including PATH, SHELL, PKG_CONFIG_PATH, CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, library paths, and all other buildtool variables — alongside metadata that allows the cache's validity to be checked cheaply. The critical invalidation condition is straightforward: if any stored environment variable contains a reference to a /nix/store/ path that does not exist on the current machine, the cache is considered stale and the full evaluation is rerun. Because Replit prepopulates a giant shared "Big Disk" with nearly all packages a user would ever request, the vast majority of REPL startups find all referenced paths present, skip evaluation entirely, and load in milliseconds.[2]

The evaluation cache therefore implements a simple but highly effective presencebased invalidation strategy: hash the set of store paths referenced by the cached environment, check their existence via the SQLite database at /nix/var/nix/db/db.sqlite, and serve the cache on a hit. This is not a sophisticated contenthash comparison of the replit.nix source itself but rather a downstream check on the outputs of evaluation. If a user edits replit.nix to add a new package not yet on the Big Disk, the new store path won't exist, the cache is invalidated, and a full evaluation + build runs.[2]

 ContentAddressable Nix Store and the Big Disk

The foundation of Replit's package delivery is a set of ~16 TB Google Cloud Persistent Disks — referred to internally as "Big Disks" — that are attached to every machine serving REPLs. Each Big Disk contains a prebuilt Nix store with close to one million software artifacts covering the full Nixpkgs collection. This shared disk is mounted readonly as the lower layer of an overlay filesystem inside every REPL container; this is what makes Replit's claim of "instant installation" of tens of thousands of packages possible without any perREPL download.[3]

The key architectural property that makes this safe for concurrent multitenant use is Nix's contentaddressable store layout: every package in /nix/store/ is placed under a directory whose name begins with a cryptographic hash of all inputs used to build it — source code hash, compiler version, all dependency hashes, build flags, etc.. Because two packages with different build inputs will always have different store paths, and because packages at a given store path are immutable once built, thousands of REPLs can share the same physical disk with no conflicts, even if they need different versions of the same library. The SQLite database at /nix/var/nix/db/db.sqlite records every valid path and its reference graph; Nix queries this database for both correctness checks and performance.[4][1][3]

Nix's inputaddressed hashing algorithm, which is the default mode used at Replit, computes the store path as a SHA256 hash over the derivation — the complete build plan including all inputs, dependencies, build scripts, and environment variables. Two derivations that are textually identical but differ in any transitive dependency will produce different hashes and therefore different store paths. This is what guarantees reproducibility: given the same replit.nix, two REPLs anywhere in the world will resolve to exactly the same set of store paths.[4]

Derivation cache invalidation flows directly from this hashing scheme: any change to replit.nix that references a different package version, a different nixpkgs revision, or adds/removes a package changes the computed derivation hash, making the prior cached output irrelevant. The .cache/replit/nix/env.json cache is then invalidated because the store paths it references will differ from the new derivation's outputs.[2]

 Tvix Store and Storage Deduplication

The Big Disk architecture worked well until the persistent disk grew to 20 TB across successive NixOS releases, driven by the need to maintain backwards compatibility with all historical store paths. Replit's response was to integrate Tvix Store, a new modular Nix store implementation from the Tvix project that is a component of a broader reimplementation of Nix.[5]

Tvix Store is backed by tvix-castore, a contentdefined chunking store that breaks all file blobs into variablesize chunks, hashes each chunk independently, and stores duplicates only once. For a Nix store containing many versions of the same package — which differ only in a few files — this achieves enormous deduplication ratios because the vast majority of chunks are shared across versions. Replit implements this by running tvix-store as a service on their container manager VMs, which exposes a FUSE filesystem that appears to containers as a normal Nix local store. Containers cannot tell the difference between a traditional /nix/store and the FUSEbacked one; the interface is identical.[5]

The result was compression of the 6 TB active cache (the most commonly accessed portion of the 20 TB disk) into 1.2 TB, a 90% reduction in storage cost for the persistent disk cache. FUSE introduces some I/O overhead compared to a native filesystem, but Replit mitigates this with FUSElevel page caching: once a chunk is read into the page cache of the storage server VM, subsequent accesses are served from RAM.[5]

 Overlay Filesystem and the Layered Store

Inside every REPL, Nix's /nix/store directory is presented through a Linux overlayfs stack with two layers:[3]

 Lower layer: the Big Disk (or Tvix Store FUSE mount), readonly, containing the prebuilt package set
 Upper layer: a perREPL scratch disk, initially empty, writable

When a REPL's replit.nix requests a package already on the Big Disk, Nix sees it in the lower layer's SQLite database, skips building, and simply adds an entry to the upper store's database indicating the package is available. The files themselves are already present on the lower layer — the overlay filesystem makes them visible through the merged view. This is the "instant installation" mechanism: no bytes are copied, no builds run, only a database entry is written.[3]

The critical limitation of the original design was that the upper scratch disk was not persistent. If a user's replit.nix triggered a Nix build of a custom package not on the Big Disk — or if they used Nix Flakes to pull in external packages — the build result was written to the upper layer but discarded when the REPL session ended. This prevented Nix Flakes and custom derivations from being useful in practice.[3]

To solve this, Replit partnered with Obsidian Systems and Tweag to implement the Local Overlay Store (Layered Store) feature for upstream Nix. The critical insight is to decouple the overlay at the database level rather than the filesystem level: instead of a single overlayfs over the entire /nix/store directory (including the database), only the /nix/store file directories are overlaid, while the upper and lower SQLite databases remain separate and independent. This allows the upper database to be persisted without conflicting with updates to the lower database (which happens when the Big Disk is rebuilt with new packages). The upper database persists between sessions; the lower database can be updated independently.[6][3]

 The nixpkgs-replit Overlay

Replit maintains a custom nixpkgs overlay called nixpkgs-replit. This is a standard Nix overlay — a function that takes the final package set and the previous package set and returns a modified package set — used to customize, patch, or add packages on top of upstream Nixpkgs. When Replit wants to add a new package to the Big Disk, an engineer adds it to nixpkgs-replit, triggers a rebuild of the Big Disk, and deploys the updated disk to all containerserving machines. The overlay system is the mechanism by which Replit exercises control over exactly which packages and versions are prebuilt and immediately available without any download delay.[3]

For packages in nixpkgs-replit, the derivation is built, cached, and served. For packages in upstream Nixpkgs that are not on the Big Disk, a REPL must trigger a Nix build against the public cache.nixos.org binary cache, which downloads the prebuilt artifact. For packages not available from any binary cache, Nix falls back to a full source build inside the REPL's overlay upper layer.

 Nixpkgs Version Pinning and Channels

Replit pins a specific revision of Nixpkgs for the "stock" REPL experience, which determines which version of each package is available via the simple pkgs.packageName syntax in replit.nix. This pinning ensures reproducibility across REPL sessions: the same replit.nix evaluated today and six months from now produces the same environment, because the underlying Nixpkgs revision is fixed.[3]

With the introduction of the Layered Store and persistent upper store, Replit opened the path to full Nix Flakes support. A Nix Flake is defined by a flake.nix file and a flake.lock lockfile that pins all external inputs (including the Nixpkgs revision) by their git commit hash and content hash. When a Nix Flake is evaluated, Nix verifies that all inputs match the hashes in the lockfile, ensuring bitforbit reproducibility regardless of when or where evaluation occurs. The lockfile is the flakesera equivalent of the old channel pinning, but with cryptographic guarantees rather than just a channel name.[3]

Before the persistent upper store became available, Nix Flake evaluation inside REPLs was problematic because any packages fetched by the flake would be discarded between sessions. With a persistent upper store, flake build results survive across sessions, making Flakes fully functional.[3]

 Nix Garbage Collection and PerREPL Store Management

Nix's standard garbage collector works by following the GC roots — a set of designated symlinks in /nix/var/nix/gcroots/ that mark which store paths are "live" — and recursively collecting all transitive dependencies of live paths. Any store path not reachable from any GC root is eligible for deletion.

At Replit's scale, the GC strategy must account for the layered architecture. The lower store (Big Disk) is managed centrally by Replit's infrastructure team: when a new Big Disk is built, packages that are no longer referenced by any current Nixpkgs revision (and are not in nixpkgs-replit) may be pruned, subject to backwards compatibility constraints. The decision to never remove any store path from the cache (for backwards compatibility with pinned REPLs) was a key constraint that drove the 20 TB disk size problem and ultimately the adoption of Tvix Store's deduplication.[5]

The upper store per REPL is bounded by the user's allocated storage quota. Custombuilt derivations accumulated in the upper store over many sessions will consume the user's storage allotment. The standard Nix GC tooling (nix-collect-garbage) can be run inside a REPL to free space. The GC roots for the REPL's development environment are typically the symlinks created by nix-shell or the nix profile activation.

 Detection of replit.nix Changes and Atomic Rebuild

The REPL runtime watches replit.nix for modifications through a standard inotifybased file watcher. When a write is detected, the environment rebuild process is triggered:

1. The cache validity check runs: does the current env.json reference store paths that still exist?
2. If yes (the modified replit.nix happens to result in the same set of paths), the cached environment is reused.
3. If no (new packages are requested), nix-shell is evaluated against the modified file.
4. If the requested packages exist on the Big Disk, they are registered in the upper database instantly.
5. If new packages need to be fetched from cache.nixos.org or built from source, this happens in the background.
6. The new environment variables are written atomically to env.json once the build is complete.
7. The REPL shell is restarted or resourced with the new environment.

The "atomic" aspect of the rebuild is that the new env.json is written as a complete replacement only after all required store paths are fully realized, preventing the REPL from entering a halfbuilt state.[2]

 Build Sandbox Techniques for Nix Derivations

When Nix builds a derivation inside a REPL, the build process runs in a sandbox enforced by Nix's builtin sandboxing features. In sandbox mode, the build process is placed in a new Linux mount namespace with only the explicitly declared inputs available; it cannot access the network, the host filesystem, or any undeclared dependencies. This is how Nix achieves its reproducibility guarantee: if a build succeeds in the sandbox with only the declared inputs, it will produce the same output anywhere those inputs are available.[3]

For Replit's multitenant environment, the Nix build sandbox runs inside an alreadycontainerized REPL environment. The container provides outer isolation (namespaces for PID, network, mount, user, IPC), and Nix's sandbox provides inner isolation for the build process within that container. The specific seccompBPF filter profiles and Landlock LSM rules applied to REPL containers are not publicly documented by Replit.



 Part II — Replit Agent Architecture

 Agent Loop: Agentic Core and Tool Execution

The Replit Agent uses an agentic loop architecture that is best characterized as a customized ReActstyle loop (Reason + Act) with significant enhancements for longhorizon reliability. The agent iterates through cycles of: reading tool outputs and context, reasoning about the current state and next action, invoking one or more tools, observing results, and repeating. Replit has not published a diagram of their exact internal state machine, but the key innovations they have disclosed publicly are:[7]

 Parallel tool calling: The agent can invoke multiple tools in a single loop iteration.[8][7]
 Decisiontime guidance injection: A classifier injects situational microinstructions before each token generation step.[7]
 Testing subagent: A separate subagent handles REPLbased verification without polluting the main agent's context.[9]
 Durable execution: Session state is persisted via Mastra + Ingest for fault tolerance during long runs.[10]

The loop runs without a fixed maximum number of steps — sessions have been documented running for over 200 continuous minutes. Context window management is the primary constraint on session length.[9]

 Tool Calling Framework

Replit Agent uses OpenAIstyle function calling (structured tool schemas with JSON arguments) as its tool invocation protocol. The Agent has access to tools including file read/write, bash command execution, web search, log reading, and the REPLbased browser testing harness. The tool schema has evolved iteratively; early versions required sequential tool calls, while current versions support parallel multitool calling — a change that delivered 15% cost savings and 30% faster results per Replit's 2025 review.[11][8][9]

When the Agent generates Playwright test code in the REPLbased verification system, it uses a code execution tool rather than calling discrete browserautomation tool endpoints. This is a deliberate architectural choice: code execution into a persistent JavaScript REPL notebook is far more tokenefficient than serializing every browser action as a separate tool call, because loops, conditionals, and multistep flows can be expressed in a single code block.[9]

 Context Management: Token Budgeting and Context Pollution

The main agent's context window fills to 80,000–100,000 tokens during complex sessions, containing file reads, code writes, tool outputs, user messages, and agent reasoning. Replit's primary strategy for managing this is subagent isolation: tasks with high context requirements (like the browser testing flow) are offloaded to separate subagents that receive only the minimal context needed for their task.[9]

The main agent communicates with the testing subagent through a highlevel plan summary, not a dump of the full context:[9]


1. Start from /products
2. Assert product displays with correct price
3. Adding to the cart works


When the subagent finishes, it returns a summarized result indicating what passed and what failed, not a transcript of the entire testing session. This keeps the roundtrip context addition small regardless of how long the testing session was.[9]

For the main agent's own context, the replit.md file (introduced in July 2025) allows users to inject persistent project context — coding style preferences, architecture decisions, environment notes — that are included in every session without requiring reexplanation.[8]

 DecisionTime Guidance and MicroInstruction Bank

One of Replit's most architecturally novel contributions is the DecisionTime Guidance system, disclosed in January 2026. The core problem it addresses is that static system prompts become ineffective on long trajectories because:[7]

 Models' learned priors from pretraining can override explicit written rules when rules are verbose or conflicting[7]
 Primacy and recency bias mean that instructions in the middle of a long context receive less attention[7]
 Adding more constraints causes diminishing returns and priority ambiguity[7]

The solution is to replace the monolithic system prompt's guidance section with a bank of reusable microinstructions — each one short, focused on a single decision, and distilled from failure patterns observed in production logs. A lightweight multilabel classifier runs on every agent iteration, analyzing the current trajectory (recent tool results, error patterns, loop indicators), and selects which microinstructions (if any) to inject at the bottom of the context window immediately before the model generates its next response.[7]

This placement at the bottom of the context exploits recency bias in a beneficial way: guidance placed at the tail end of the trace exerts disproportionately strong influence on the next generated token. Injecting guidance for parallel tool calling at the end of the trace rather than in the system prompt produced 15% more tool calls per loop.[7]

Critically, injected microinstructions are ephemeral: they do not persist in conversation history after the current step. This prevents context accumulation from the guidance itself. The core system prompt never changes, which means the prompt cache is always hit for that portion, reducing cost  — Replit reports a 90% cost reduction compared to dynamic systemprompt modification.[7]

The classifier's falsepositive rate is intentionally acceptable: since microinstructions are framed as suggestions rather than hard constraints, the model will simply ignore injected guidance that doesn't apply to the current decision. Replit therefore tunes the classifier for recall over precision: better to occasionally inject an irrelevant reminder than to miss a real failure mode.[7]

 Doom Loop Detection and the Consultant Agent

A specific pattern the classifier is trained to detect is the "doom loop" — a trajectory where the agent makes repeated failed attempts at the same fix, performs circular edits, or makes highrisk changes without progress. When a doom loop is detected, the system injects a reminder prompting the main agent to consult an external consultant agent.[7]

The consultant agent is invoked with fresh context — it does not see the polluted trajectory of failed attempts that has confused the main agent. It generates a plan from scratch and returns it to the main agent. The stuck agent's task is then reduced to recognizing a good plan when offered one, which is the easier task compared to generating its way out of a failure state. This exploits what Replit cites as the "generatordiscriminator gap": the same model that cannot generate a correct solution can often recognize one.[7]

Replit uses a different model for the consultant agent than the main agent. This reduces selfpreference bias — the tendency of a model used as both generator and evaluator to favor its own previous outputs even when they are wrong.[7]

 SelfTesting Subagent: REPLBased Verification

Agent 3's most distinctive capability is its ability to autonomously verify its own code through browser automation. This addresses the problem of "Potemkin interfaces" — applications that look functional on first inspection (buttons render, dashboards display numbers, UI responds to clicks) but are fundamentally broken (event handlers missing, data mocked, links going nowhere).[9]

The verification system has three components:

Code Use (Playwright in a persistent REPL)

Rather than using a browserautomation framework as a set of discrete tool endpoints (which limits expressivity and consumes peraction tokens), Replit gives the testing subagent a persistent JavaScript REPL notebook with Playwright available as an injectable library. The agent writes Playwright code that is executed in the notebook's persistent context. Variables, browser sessions, cookies, and local state all persist between code executions within the same testing session.[9]

This enables patterns that are impossible with peraction tool calls:

javascript
// execution 1: capture order ID from purchase flow
let orderID = await completePurchase(cart);
console.log("Order placed");

// execution 2: use the persisted orderID from execution 1
await page.getByLabel('orderNumber').fill(orderID);
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();


Token efficiency via code is also dramatic. A 36month calendar navigation that would require 36 sequential model calls with peraction browser use becomes a single model call generating a for loop. Multitab stateful flows (e.g., booking on tab 1 + verifying availability on tab 2) are expressed as normal concurrent JavaScript, not as a long sequence of individual tool calls.[9]

Augmented DOM and Database Access

The testing subagent receives a strippeddown DOM representation augmented with ARIA labels and data-test attributes. Replit prompts the main agent during code generation to add these attributes to interactive elements, making them reliably targetable in tests without fragile CSS selectors. The subagent also has access to readonly database query utilities injected into the REPL context, allowing it to verify that backend state changed as expected after a UI interaction. Realtime client and server logs captured since the last execution are also provided, enabling causeeffect debugging.[9]

Subagent Communication Protocol

The testing subagent receives a highlevel plan from the main agent (3–5 bullet points describing the flows to test), executes the testing session in its own context window, and returns a summarized report of what passed and what failed with specific error descriptions. The protocol is deliberately minimal to prevent context pollution in both directions.[9]

Cost and Performance

The hybrid approach achieves a median test cost of $0.20 per session. This compares favorably to the rough estimate of $0.50 and 30–90 seconds just to fill out a 5field form using a visionbased computeruse agent operating on pixels. The advantage comes from code's token efficiency: loops replace perstep model calls, persistent state reduces renavigation, and Playwright's strong representation in LLM training data means the model generates correct automation code without extensive prompting.[9]

 Agent 3 Autonomy: 200+ Minutes

The combination of decisiontime guidance, the testing subagent, and durable execution (via Mastra + Ingest for faulttolerant workflow orchestration) enabled Agent 3 to operate productively for over 200 continuous minutes without human intervention. This is roughly 10x the ~20minute horizon of earlier agent versions. Success rate for complete durable execution sessions improved from 80% to 96% with the addition of Mastra + Ingest.[10][9]

 Agent Modes and Planning

Replit's agent surface exposes different planning behaviors. "Plan mode" (introduced with expanded proactivity in October 2025) allows the Agent to suggest task lists proactively rather than waiting for explicit user direction. The Agent Queue system (July 2025) lets the Agent automatically organize multiple requests into a prioritized task list.[12][8]

The July 2025 introduction of replit.md as a custom agent instructions file allows users to configure Agent behavior with projectspecific context: coding style preferences, architectural constraints, environment notes. This is the primary mechanism for crosssession state persistence beyond what is captured in git history.[8]

 AgentGenerated replit.nix Files

When the Agent determines that a new package is needed — either from a user request or its own inference during code generation — it modifies replit.nix directly using its fileedit tool. The modified file is written to the REPL's filesystem, the inotify watcher detects the change, and the environment rebuild process described above is triggered. The Agent generates valid Nix expressions because Nixpkgs package names are wellrepresented in its training data and because the structure of replit.nix is a simple attribute list.[3]

For example, if a user asks for a Python REPL with scientific computing packages, the Agent might generate:

nix
{ pkgs }: {
  deps = [
    pkgs.python311
    pkgs.python311Packages.numpy
    pkgs.python311Packages.scipy
    pkgs.python311Packages.matplotlib
  ];
}


The Agent validates that the packages it references exist in the Nixpkgs version pinned by the REPL's channel, drawing on its knowledge of the Nixpkgs attribute tree. For complex environments (custom builds, specific version pins, overlays), the Agent can generate more sophisticated expressions using pkgs.mkShell, pkgs.stdenv.mkDerivation, or flakestyle configurations.



 Part III — Snapshot Engine and Storage Architecture

 Bottomless Storage: 16 MiB CoW Block Devices

Every Replit application's filesystem is backed by a virtual block device served via the Network Block Device (NBD) protocol from storage servers colocated with the VM/container running the app. These storage servers act as caching proxies between the app and Google Cloud Storage (GCS), where the actual data lives.[13]

Each block device is divided into 16 MiB immutable chunks stored in GCS. A manifest file records the ordered list of chunk references (GCS object identifiers) that constitute the current version of the block device. Because chunks are immutable, copying a disk is only a manifest copy — a constanttime O(1) operation regardless of how large the disk is. A 1 GB filesystem and a 100 GB filesystem take the same time to "fork" because forking only copies the manifest.[14][13]

When data is written to a block device (e.g., a user saves a file), the affected 16 MiB chunk is read from GCS (if not already in the local cache), the write is applied in memory, and the modified chunk is written as a new, differently named immutable object in GCS. The manifest is updated to point to the new chunk. Old chunks are not deleted; they remain in GCS and are referenced by previous manifest versions. This is the CopyonWrite property: forks of the same disk share all unmodified chunks and only diverge in the chunks that are written after the fork.[13][14]

The storage servers maintain a local disk cache of recently accessed GCS chunks to reduce latency; chunk reads that hit the local cache return at disk speeds rather than GCS network latency. This lazyloading strategy means that even a 100 GB block device can be started and used immediately — only the chunks that are actually accessed are fetched from GCS.[13]

 Forkable Postgres Databases

The same 16 MiB CoW block device infrastructure is used to make PostgreSQL databases forkable. Replit runs a standard, unmodified local Postgres instance whose data directory sits on a block device backed by Bottomless Storage. This means:[13]

 Checkpoint = copy the current manifest under a new name (takes milliseconds, sizeindependent)
 Restore = replace the current manifest with a previous version (also milliseconds)
 Fork = create a new manifest copy; the forked Postgres instance starts with identical data to the original

The WAL (WriteAhead Log) is not specially handled — it is simply part of the Postgres data directory and is therefore subject to the same filesystemlevel snapshotting. When a database is restored to a checkpoint, the WAL state at that checkpoint is also restored, ensuring Postgres can start cleanly from a consistent state.[13]

 Agent Checkpoints

During an Agent session, checkpoints combine a git commit (versioning the code) with a manifest snapshot (versioning the database). Both operations are fast: the git commit uses standard git object storage, and the manifest snapshot is the constanttime CoW copy. If a user dislikes a set of Agent changes, they roll back to any checkpoint, which restores both the codebase (via git) and the database (via manifest swap) to the state at that checkpoint.[13]

Replit maintains a separate, immutable, appendonly git remote for every application, so even if the Agent corrupts the git state inside the REPL's filesystem, the entire git history can be recovered from the external remote.[13]

 Parallel Simulations

The snapshot architecture enables parallel trajectory exploration for the Agent. By taking a snapshot and forking both the filesystem and database, multiple Agent instances can be launched simultaneously against the same initial state. Each instance explores a different approach to solving a problem. Because the Nix store snapshot is also included in the filesystem fork, each parallel Agent has a consistent, complete development environment without any additional setup.[13]

At the end of parallel exploration, the best result is applied atomically to the production state. Replit cites a parallel sampling technique derived from inferencetime scaling and references SWEbench performance improvements of ~8 percentage points (72% → 80%) from this approach.[13]



 Part IV — Security Architecture

 AIGenerated Code Security

Replit's January 2026 white paper on securing AIgenerated code concludes that AIonly security scans are insufficient for production use. Key findings:[15]

 Functionally equivalent code with minor syntactic differences (variable names, formatting) receives different security classifications from LLMbased scanners[15]
 Dependencylevel CVEs are essentially invisible to LLMs because they require access to continuously updated vulnerability feeds (NVD, OSV, GitHub Security Advisories)[15]
 Detection depends on prompt phrasing: if a security issue type is not explicitly mentioned in the scan prompt, it is likely missed[15]
 Static analysis tools deliver deterministic, repeatable detection regardless of syntactic variation[15]

Replit's production security architecture therefore uses a hybrid approach: deterministic static analysis and dependency scanning establish a reliable baseline, while LLMbased reasoning is applied on top for businesslogic and intentlevel issues that rulebased scanners cannot catch.[15]

 Sandboxing and Isolation

Replit's REPL isolation uses Linux namespaces (mount, PID, network, user, IPC) to provide containerlevel isolation between user workloads. The specific configuration details — which seccompBPF syscall filter profiles are applied, whether gVisor or Firecracker microVMs are used for any tier of REPL, the exact cgroup v2 controller configurations — have not been publicly disclosed by Replit.

The Agent operates with restricted database access: it can only write to the development database, never the production database. This is enforced at the infrastructure level, not purely by prompt instruction. The development/production split is a hard boundary that prevents Agentinduced data loss in production.[13]

For the parallel simulation sandboxes, Replit notes that they plan to relax some model guardrails in the isolated simulation environments specifically, since any destructive actions are safely contained and can be discarded. This means the Agent in a sandbox can be given more latitude (e.g., adding log statements, making temporary schema changes, installing debugging tools) than it would be in the normal development environment.[13]



 Part V — EndtoEnd Agent + Nix Flow

 Full RequesttoCommit Flow

The complete flow from a user request to a committed application state proceeds roughly as follows:[3][13][9][7]

1. User Request: The user types a naturallanguage request in the Agent interface. The Agent receives the request along with its full context window (current files, recent conversation, project replit.md instructions).

2. Planning: The Agent generates a task list (shown to the user in Plan mode) or begins executing directly. For complex requests, it may use a separate highlevel planning step to decompose the task into subtasks.

3. Nix Environment Provisioning: If the Agent determines that new packages are required (e.g., the user wants a Rust project and the REPL doesn't have Rust), it edits replit.nix using the filewrite tool. The environment watcher detects the change and triggers evaluation. If the package is on the Big Disk, it is registered instantly. If not, a build/fetch runs in the background.

4. Code Generation and Tool Execution: The Agent iterates through its ReAct loop, generating code files using the edit tool and executing bash commands using the shell tool. At each step, the DecisionTime Guidance classifier analyzes the trajectory and injects relevant microinstructions.

5. REPLBased Verification: When a significant feature is complete, the Agent launches the testing subagent with a highlevel test plan. The subagent executes Playwright code in the persistent JavaScript REPL, verifies behavior against the database, reads logs, and returns a pass/fail summary.

6. Reflection and Correction: If tests fail, the main agent receives the failure summary and enters a correction loop. If a doom loop is detected, the consultant agent is invoked for a fresh plan.

7. Checkpoint / State Commit: When the Agent reaches a "done" state for a task (either because tests pass or because the user confirms), a checkpoint is created: a git commit records the code state, and a manifest copy records the database state. Both operations are fast and atomic.[13]

Replit's Nix and Agent infrastructure is one of the most extensively engineered but partially documented platforms in the developertools space. Below is the most comprehensive public synthesis available, drawing directly from Replit's engineering blog posts, opensource contributions, and technical disclosures. Where Replit has not publicly documented specific internals, that boundary is clearly marked.



 Part I — Replit's Nix Infrastructure

 Nix Evaluator Backend

Replit uses the standard upstream C++ Nix evaluator — not a custom reimplementation — to process replit.nix files. The evaluator is invoked through nix-shell, which evaluates the derivation expression and resolves all package closures into a set of /nix/store/ paths. There is no evidence Replit has written a custom Nix evaluator from scratch; their engineering work has focused instead on the caching layer that sits above the evaluator, and on the store architecture below it.[1]

The most significant performance innovation Replit made to the evaluation path is the environment variable cache, stored at .cache/replit/nix/env.json inside every REPL's filesystem. Prior to this optimization, every REPL startup triggered a full nix-shell evaluation of replit.nix, which could consume seconds to tens of seconds of wallclock time. The cached JSON file stores the entire set of environment variables that nix-shell would produce — including PATH, SHELL, PKG_CONFIG_PATH, CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, library paths, and all other buildtool variables — alongside metadata that allows the cache's validity to be checked cheaply. The critical invalidation condition is straightforward: if any stored environment variable contains a reference to a /nix/store/ path that does not exist on the current machine, the cache is considered stale and the full evaluation is rerun. Because Replit prepopulates a giant shared "Big Disk" with nearly all packages a user would ever request, the vast majority of REPL startups find all referenced paths present, skip evaluation entirely, and load in milliseconds.[2]

The evaluation cache therefore implements a simple but highly effective presencebased invalidation strategy: hash the set of store paths referenced by the cached environment, check their existence via the SQLite database at /nix/var/nix/db/db.sqlite, and serve the cache on a hit. This is not a sophisticated contenthash comparison of the replit.nix source itself but rather a downstream check on the outputs of evaluation. If a user edits replit.nix to add a new package not yet on the Big Disk, the new store path won't exist, the cache is invalidated, and a full evaluation + build runs.[2]

 ContentAddressable Nix Store and the Big Disk

The foundation of Replit's package delivery is a set of ~16 TB Google Cloud Persistent Disks — referred to internally as "Big Disks" — that are attached to every machine serving REPLs. Each Big Disk contains a prebuilt Nix store with close to one million software artifacts covering the full Nixpkgs collection. This shared disk is mounted readonly as the lower layer of an overlay filesystem inside every REPL container; this is what makes Replit's claim of "instant installation" of tens of thousands of packages possible without any perREPL download.[3]

The key architectural property that makes this safe for concurrent multitenant use is Nix's contentaddressable store layout: every package in /nix/store/ is placed under a directory whose name begins with a cryptographic hash of all inputs used to build it — source code hash, compiler version, all dependency hashes, build flags, etc.. Because two packages with different build inputs will always have different store paths, and because packages at a given store path are immutable once built, thousands of REPLs can share the same physical disk with no conflicts, even if they need different versions of the same library. The SQLite database at /nix/var/nix/db/db.sqlite records every valid path and its reference graph; Nix queries this database for both correctness checks and performance.[4][1][3]

Nix's inputaddressed hashing algorithm, which is the default mode used at Replit, computes the store path as a SHA256 hash over the derivation — the complete build plan including all inputs, dependencies, build scripts, and environment variables. Two derivations that are textually identical but differ in any transitive dependency will produce different hashes and therefore different store paths. This is what guarantees reproducibility: given the same replit.nix, two REPLs anywhere in the world will resolve to exactly the same set of store paths.[4]

Derivation cache invalidation flows directly from this hashing scheme: any change to replit.nix that references a different package version, a different nixpkgs revision, or adds/removes a package changes the computed derivation hash, making the prior cached output irrelevant. The .cache/replit/nix/env.json cache is then invalidated because the store paths it references will differ from the new derivation's outputs.[2]

 Tvix Store and Storage Deduplication

The Big Disk architecture worked well until the persistent disk grew to 20 TB across successive NixOS releases, driven by the need to maintain backwards compatibility with all historical store paths. Replit's response was to integrate Tvix Store, a new modular Nix store implementation from the Tvix project that is a component of a broader reimplementation of Nix.[5]

Tvix Store is backed by tvix-castore, a contentdefined chunking store that breaks all file blobs into variablesize chunks, hashes each chunk independently, and stores duplicates only once. For a Nix store containing many versions of the same package — which differ only in a few files — this achieves enormous deduplication ratios because the vast majority of chunks are shared across versions. Replit implements this by running tvix-store as a service on their container manager VMs, which exposes a FUSE filesystem that appears to containers as a normal Nix local store. Containers cannot tell the difference between a traditional /nix/store and the FUSEbacked one; the interface is identical.[5]

The result was compression of the 6 TB active cache (the most commonly accessed portion of the 20 TB disk) into 1.2 TB, a 90% reduction in storage cost for the persistent disk cache. FUSE introduces some I/O overhead compared to a native filesystem, but Replit mitigates this with FUSElevel page caching: once a chunk is read into the page cache of the storage server VM, subsequent accesses are served from RAM.[5]

 Overlay Filesystem and the Layered Store

Inside every REPL, Nix's /nix/store directory is presented through a Linux overlayfs stack with two layers:[3]

 Lower layer: the Big Disk (or Tvix Store FUSE mount), readonly, containing the prebuilt package set
 Upper layer: a perREPL scratch disk, initially empty, writable

When a REPL's replit.nix requests a package already on the Big Disk, Nix sees it in the lower layer's SQLite database, skips building, and simply adds an entry to the upper store's database indicating the package is available. The files themselves are already present on the lower layer — the overlay filesystem makes them visible through the merged view. This is the "instant installation" mechanism: no bytes are copied, no builds run, only a database entry is written.[3]

The critical limitation of the original design was that the upper scratch disk was not persistent. If a user's replit.nix triggered a Nix build of a custom package not on the Big Disk — or if they used Nix Flakes to pull in external packages — the build result was written to the upper layer but discarded when the REPL session ended. This prevented Nix Flakes and custom derivations from being useful in practice.[3]

To solve this, Replit partnered with Obsidian Systems and Tweag to implement the Local Overlay Store (Layered Store) feature for upstream Nix. The critical insight is to decouple the overlay at the database level rather than the filesystem level: instead of a single overlayfs over the entire /nix/store directory (including the database), only the /nix/store file directories are overlaid, while the upper and lower SQLite databases remain separate and independent. This allows the upper database to be persisted without conflicting with updates to the lower database (which happens when the Big Disk is rebuilt with new packages). The upper database persists between sessions; the lower database can be updated independently.[6][3]

 The nixpkgs-replit Overlay

Replit maintains a custom nixpkgs overlay called nixpkgs-replit. This is a standard Nix overlay — a function that takes the final package set and the previous package set and returns a modified package set — used to customize, patch, or add packages on top of upstream Nixpkgs. When Replit wants to add a new package to the Big Disk, an engineer adds it to nixpkgs-replit, triggers a rebuild of the Big Disk, and deploys the updated disk to all containerserving machines. The overlay system is the mechanism by which Replit exercises control over exactly which packages and versions are prebuilt and immediately available without any download delay.[3]

For packages in nixpkgs-replit, the derivation is built, cached, and served. For packages in upstream Nixpkgs that are not on the Big Disk, a REPL must trigger a Nix build against the public cache.nixos.org binary cache, which downloads the prebuilt artifact. For packages not available from any binary cache, Nix falls back to a full source build inside the REPL's overlay upper layer.

 Nixpkgs Version Pinning and Channels

Replit pins a specific revision of Nixpkgs for the "stock" REPL experience, which determines which version of each package is available via the simple pkgs.packageName syntax in replit.nix. This pinning ensures reproducibility across REPL sessions: the same replit.nix evaluated today and six months from now produces the same environment, because the underlying Nixpkgs revision is fixed.[3]

With the introduction of the Layered Store and persistent upper store, Replit opened the path to full Nix Flakes support. A Nix Flake is defined by a flake.nix file and a flake.lock lockfile that pins all external inputs (including the Nixpkgs revision) by their git commit hash and content hash. When a Nix Flake is evaluated, Nix verifies that all inputs match the hashes in the lockfile, ensuring bitforbit reproducibility regardless of when or where evaluation occurs. The lockfile is the flakesera equivalent of the old channel pinning, but with cryptographic guarantees rather than just a channel name.[3]

Before the persistent upper store became available, Nix Flake evaluation inside REPLs was problematic because any packages fetched by the flake would be discarded between sessions. With a persistent upper store, flake build results survive across sessions, making Flakes fully functional.[3]

 Nix Garbage Collection and PerREPL Store Management

Nix's standard garbage collector works by following the GC roots — a set of designated symlinks in /nix/var/nix/gcroots/ that mark which store paths are "live" — and recursively collecting all transitive dependencies of live paths. Any store path not reachable from any GC root is eligible for deletion.

At Replit's scale, the GC strategy must account for the layered architecture. The lower store (Big Disk) is managed centrally by Replit's infrastructure team: when a new Big Disk is built, packages that are no longer referenced by any current Nixpkgs revision (and are not in nixpkgs-replit) may be pruned, subject to backwards compatibility constraints. The decision to never remove any store path from the cache (for backwards compatibility with pinned REPLs) was a key constraint that drove the 20 TB disk size problem and ultimately the adoption of Tvix Store's deduplication.[5]

The upper store per REPL is bounded by the user's allocated storage quota. Custombuilt derivations accumulated in the upper store over many sessions will consume the user's storage allotment. The standard Nix GC tooling (nix-collect-garbage) can be run inside a REPL to free space. The GC roots for the REPL's development environment are typically the symlinks created by nix-shell or the nix profile activation.

 Detection of replit.nix Changes and Atomic Rebuild

The REPL runtime watches replit.nix for modifications through a standard inotifybased file watcher. When a write is detected, the environment rebuild process is triggered:

1. The cache validity check runs: does the current env.json reference store paths that still exist?
2. If yes (the modified replit.nix happens to result in the same set of paths), the cached environment is reused.
3. If no (new packages are requested), nix-shell is evaluated against the modified file.
4. If the requested packages exist on the Big Disk, they are registered in the upper database instantly.
5. If new packages need to be fetched from cache.nixos.org or built from source, this happens in the background.
6. The new environment variables are written atomically to env.json once the build is complete.
7. The REPL shell is restarted or resourced with the new environment.

The "atomic" aspect of the rebuild is that the new env.json is written as a complete replacement only after all required store paths are fully realized, preventing the REPL from entering a halfbuilt state.[2]

 Build Sandbox Techniques for Nix Derivations

When Nix builds a derivation inside a REPL, the build process runs in a sandbox enforced by Nix's builtin sandboxing features. In sandbox mode, the build process is placed in a new Linux mount namespace with only the explicitly declared inputs available; it cannot access the network, the host filesystem, or any undeclared dependencies. This is how Nix achieves its reproducibility guarantee: if a build succeeds in the sandbox with only the declared inputs, it will produce the same output anywhere those inputs are available.[3]

For Replit's multitenant environment, the Nix build sandbox runs inside an alreadycontainerized REPL environment. The container provides outer isolation (namespaces for PID, network, mount, user, IPC), and Nix's sandbox provides inner isolation for the build process within that container. The specific seccompBPF filter profiles and Landlock LSM rules applied to REPL containers are not publicly documented by Replit.



 Part II — Replit Agent Architecture

 Agent Loop: Agentic Core and Tool Execution

The Replit Agent uses an agentic loop architecture that is best characterized as a customized ReActstyle loop (Reason + Act) with significant enhancements for longhorizon reliability. The agent iterates through cycles of: reading tool outputs and context, reasoning about the current state and next action, invoking one or more tools, observing results, and repeating. Replit has not published a diagram of their exact internal state machine, but the key innovations they have disclosed publicly are:[7]

 Parallel tool calling: The agent can invoke multiple tools in a single loop iteration.[8][7]
 Decisiontime guidance injection: A classifier injects situational microinstructions before each token generation step.[7]
 Testing subagent: A separate subagent handles REPLbased verification without polluting the main agent's context.[9]
 Durable execution: Session state is persisted via Mastra + Ingest for fault tolerance during long runs.[10]

The loop runs without a fixed maximum number of steps — sessions have been documented running for over 200 continuous minutes. Context window management is the primary constraint on session length.[9]

 Tool Calling Framework

Replit Agent uses OpenAIstyle function calling (structured tool schemas with JSON arguments) as its tool invocation protocol. The Agent has access to tools including file read/write, bash command execution, web search, log reading, and the REPLbased browser testing harness. The tool schema has evolved iteratively; early versions required sequential tool calls, while current versions support parallel multitool calling — a change that delivered 15% cost savings and 30% faster results per Replit's 2025 review.[11][8][9]

When the Agent generates Playwright test code in the REPLbased verification system, it uses a code execution tool rather than calling discrete browserautomation tool endpoints. This is a deliberate architectural choice: code execution into a persistent JavaScript REPL notebook is far more tokenefficient than serializing every browser action as a separate tool call, because loops, conditionals, and multistep flows can be expressed in a single code block.[9]

 Context Management: Token Budgeting and Context Pollution

The main agent's context window fills to 80,000–100,000 tokens during complex sessions, containing file reads, code writes, tool outputs, user messages, and agent reasoning. Replit's primary strategy for managing this is subagent isolation: tasks with high context requirements (like the browser testing flow) are offloaded to separate subagents that receive only the minimal context needed for their task.[9]

The main agent communicates with the testing subagent through a highlevel plan summary, not a dump of the full context:[9]


1. Start from /products
2. Assert product displays with correct price
3. Adding to the cart works


When the subagent finishes, it returns a summarized result indicating what passed and what failed, not a transcript of the entire testing session. This keeps the roundtrip context addition small regardless of how long the testing session was.[9]

For the main agent's own context, the replit.md file (introduced in July 2025) allows users to inject persistent project context — coding style preferences, architecture decisions, environment notes — that are included in every session without requiring reexplanation.[8]

 DecisionTime Guidance and MicroInstruction Bank

One of Replit's most architecturally novel contributions is the DecisionTime Guidance system, disclosed in January 2026. The core problem it addresses is that static system prompts become ineffective on long trajectories because:[7]

 Models' learned priors from pretraining can override explicit written rules when rules are verbose or conflicting[7]
 Primacy and recency bias mean that instructions in the middle of a long context receive less attention[7]
 Adding more constraints causes diminishing returns and priority ambiguity[7]

The solution is to replace the monolithic system prompt's guidance section with a bank of reusable microinstructions — each one short, focused on a single decision, and distilled from failure patterns observed in production logs. A lightweight multilabel classifier runs on every agent iteration, analyzing the current trajectory (recent tool results, error patterns, loop indicators), and selects which microinstructions (if any) to inject at the bottom of the context window immediately before the model generates its next response.[7]

This placement at the bottom of the context exploits recency bias in a beneficial way: guidance placed at the tail end of the trace exerts disproportionately strong influence on the next generated token. Injecting guidance for parallel tool calling at the end of the trace rather than in the system prompt produced 15% more tool calls per loop.[7]

Critically, injected microinstructions are ephemeral: they do not persist in conversation history after the current step. This prevents context accumulation from the guidance itself. The core system prompt never changes, which means the prompt cache is always hit for that portion, reducing cost  — Replit reports a 90% cost reduction compared to dynamic systemprompt modification.[7]

The classifier's falsepositive rate is intentionally acceptable: since microinstructions are framed as suggestions rather than hard constraints, the model will simply ignore injected guidance that doesn't apply to the current decision. Replit therefore tunes the classifier for recall over precision: better to occasionally inject an irrelevant reminder than to miss a real failure mode.[7]

 Doom Loop Detection and the Consultant Agent

A specific pattern the classifier is trained to detect is the "doom loop" — a trajectory where the agent makes repeated failed attempts at the same fix, performs circular edits, or makes highrisk changes without progress. When a doom loop is detected, the system injects a reminder prompting the main agent to consult an external consultant agent.[7]

The consultant agent is invoked with fresh context — it does not see the polluted trajectory of failed attempts that has confused the main agent. It generates a plan from scratch and returns it to the main agent. The stuck agent's task is then reduced to recognizing a good plan when offered one, which is the easier task compared to generating its way out of a failure state. This exploits what Replit cites as the "generatordiscriminator gap": the same model that cannot generate a correct solution can often recognize one.[7]

Replit uses a different model for the consultant agent than the main agent. This reduces selfpreference bias — the tendency of a model used as both generator and evaluator to favor its own previous outputs even when they are wrong.[7]

Agent 3's most distinctive capability is its ability to autonomously verify its own code through browser automation. This addresses the problem of "Potemkin interfaces" — applications that look functional on first inspection (buttons render, dashboards display numbers, UI responds to clicks) but are fundamentally broken (event handlers missing, data mocked, links going nowhere).[9]

 Part III — Snapshot Engine and Storage Architecture

 Bottomless Storage: 16 MiB CoW Block Devices

Every Replit application's filesystem is backed by a virtual block device served via the Network Block Device (NBD) protocol from storage servers colocated with the VM/container running the app. These storage servers act as caching proxies between the app and Google Cloud Storage (GCS), where the actual data lives.[13]

Each block device is divided into 16 MiB immutable chunks stored in GCS. A manifest file records the ordered list of chunk references (GCS object identifiers) that constitute the current version of the block device. Because chunks are immutable, copying a disk is only a manifest copy — a constanttime O(1) operation regardless of how large the disk is. A 1 GB filesystem and a 100 GB filesystem take the same time to "fork" because forking only copies the manifest.[14][13]

When data is written to a block device (e.g., a user saves a file), the affected 16 MiB chunk is read from GCS (if not already in the local cache), the write is applied in memory, and the modified chunk is written as a new, differently named immutable object in GCS. The manifest is updated to point to the new chunk. Old chunks are not deleted; they remain in GCS and are referenced by previous manifest versions. This is the CopyonWrite property: forks of the same disk share all unmodified chunks and only diverge in the chunks that are written after the fork.[13][14]

The storage servers maintain a local disk cache of recently accessed GCS chunks to reduce latency; chunk reads that hit the local cache return at disk speeds rather than GCS network latency. This lazyloading strategy means that even a 100 GB block device can be started and used immediately — only the chunks that are actually accessed are fetched from GCS.[13]

 Forkable Postgres Databases

The same 16 MiB CoW block device infrastructure is used to make PostgreSQL databases forkable. Replit runs a standard, unmodified local Postgres instance whose data directory sits on a block device backed by Bottomless Storage. This means:[13]

 Checkpoint = copy the current manifest under a new name (takes milliseconds, sizeindependent)
 Restore = replace the current manifest with a previous version (also milliseconds)
 Fork = create a new manifest copy; the forked Postgres instance starts with identical data to the original

The WAL (WriteAhead Log) is not specially handled — it is simply part of the Postgres data directory and is therefore subject to the same filesystemlevel snapshotting. When a database is restored to a checkpoint, the WAL state at that checkpoint is also restored, ensuring Postgres can start cleanly from a consistent state.[13]

 Agent Checkpoints

During an Agent session, checkpoints combine a git commit (versioning the code) with a manifest snapshot (versioning the database). Both operations are fast: the git commit uses standard git object storage, and the manifest snapshot is the constanttime CoW copy. If a user dislikes a set of Agent changes, they roll back to any checkpoint, which restores both the codebase (via git) and the database (via manifest swap) to the state at that checkpoint.[13]

Replit maintains a separate, immutable, appendonly git remote for every application, so even if the Agent corrupts the git state inside the REPL's filesystem, the entire git history can be recovered from the external remote.[13]

 Parallel Simulations

The snapshot architecture enables parallel trajectory exploration for the Agent. By taking a snapshot and forking both the filesystem and database, multiple Agent instances can be launched simultaneously against the same initial state. Each instance explores a different approach to solving a problem. Because the Nix store snapshot is also included in the filesystem fork, each parallel Agent has a consistent, complete development environment without any additional setup.[13]

At the end of parallel exploration, the best result is applied atomically to the production state. Replit cites a parallel sampling technique derived from inferencetime scaling and references SWEbench performance improvements of ~8 percentage points (72% → 80%) from this approach.[13]

 AIGenerated Code Security

Replit's January 2026 white paper on securing AIgenerated code concludes that AIonly security scans are insufficient for production use. Key findings:[15]

 Functionally equivalent code with minor syntactic differences (variable names, formatting) receives different security classifications from LLMbased scanners[15]
 Dependencylevel CVEs are essentially invisible to LLMs because they require access to continuously updated vulnerability feeds (NVD, OSV, GitHub Security Advisories)[15]
 Detection depends on prompt phrasing: if a security issue type is not explicitly mentioned in the scan prompt, it is likely missed[15]
 Static analysis tools deliver deterministic, repeatable detection regardless of syntactic variation[15]

Replit's production security architecture therefore uses a hybrid approach: deterministic static analysis and dependency scanning establish a reliable baseline, while LLMbased reasoning is applied on top for businesslogic and intentlevel issues that rulebased scanners cannot catch.[15]

 Sandboxing and Isolation

Replit's REPL isolation uses Linux namespaces (mount, PID, network, user, IPC) to provide containerlevel isolation between user workloads. The specific configuration details — which seccompBPF syscall filter profiles are applied, whether gVisor or Firecracker microVMs are used for any tier of REPL, the exact cgroup v2 controller configurations — have not been publicly disclosed by Replit.

The Agent operates with restricted database access: it can only write to the development database, never the production database. This is enforced at the infrastructure level, not purely by prompt instruction. The development/production split is a hard boundary that prevents Agentinduced data loss in production.[13]

For the parallel simulation sandboxes, Replit notes that they plan to relax some model guardrails in the isolated simulation environments specifically, since any destructive actions are safely contained and can be discarded. This means the Agent in a sandbox can be given more latitude (e.g., adding log statements, making temporary schema changes, installing debugging tools) than it would be in the normal development environment.[13]



 Part V — EndtoEnd Agent + Nix Flow

 Full RequesttoCommit Flow

The complete flow from a user request to a committed application state proceeds roughly as follows:[3][13][9][7]

1. User Request: The user types a naturallanguage request in the Agent interface. The Agent receives the request along with its full context window (current files, recent conversation, project replit.md instructions).

2. Planning: The Agent generates a task list (shown to the user in Plan mode) or begins executing directly. For complex requests, it may use a separate highlevel planning step to decompose the task into subtasks.

3. Nix Environment Provisioning: If the Agent determines that new packages are required (e.g., the user wants a Rust project and the REPL doesn't have Rust), it edits replit.nix using the filewrite tool. The environment watcher detects the change and triggers evaluation. If the package is on the Big Disk, it is registered instantly. If not, a build/fetch runs in the background.

4. Code Generation and Tool Execution: The Agent iterates through its ReAct loop, generating code files using the edit tool and executing bash commands using the shell tool. At each step, the DecisionTime Guidance classifier analyzes the trajectory and injects relevant microinstructions.

5. REPLBased Verification: When a significant feature is complete, the Agent launches the testing subagent with a highlevel test plan. The subagent executes Playwright code in the persistent JavaScript REPL, verifies behavior against the database, reads logs, and returns a pass/fail summary.

6. Reflection and Correction: If tests fail, the main agent receives the failure summary and enters a correction loop. If a doom loop is detected, the consultant agent is invoked for a fresh plan.

7. Checkpoint / State Commit: When the Agent reaches a "done" state for a task (either because tests pass or because the user confirms), a checkpoint is created: a git commit records the code state, and a manifest copy records the database state. Both operations are fast and atomic.[13]

8. Observability: Throughout the session, tool executions, model calls, and agent state transitions are instrumented. Replit uses durable execution via Mastra + Ingest to ensure that even network failures or infrastructure interruptions during a long session do not cause the Agent to lose progress or corrupt state.[10]

4. Get the current git HEAD commit hash via git.Repo(project_dir).head.commit.hexsha (or None if no commits).

 III.15 — Main Agent Loop

Implement an AgentLoop class. Its constructor accepts all service dependencies: BedrockClaudeClient, GLM5Client, KimiClient, AgentToolRegistry, DTGClassifier, DragonflyDB, config.

Implement async def run(self, session_id: str, project_id: str, user_message: str, mode: str, ws_send: Callable) as the primary entry point. ws_send is an async callable that sends a serialized WebSocketMessage to the connected client WebSocket. The method implements the complete agent loop:

Step 1 — Session Setup: Load or create AgentSession from Dragonfly. Load conversation history from agent:{session_id}:history. Append the new user message. Load agent.md from the project directory and prepend its contents to the system prompt.

Step 2 — System Prompt Construction: Build the system prompt as a multisection string. It must include:
 A description of the agent's role: "You are an expert software engineer working autonomously in a cloudbased development environment. Your task is to implement the user's request fully and completely."
 The current mode: Plan, Build, or Max Autonomy, with modespecific behavioral guidance.
 The project's agent.md content (if it exists and is nonempty), clearly delimited.
 A description of all available tools and when to use each.
 The rule: "Always use multiple tool calls in a single response when independent operations can be parallelized."
 The rule: "Never declare a task complete without running the browser_test tool or the appropriate test runner to verify runtime behavior."
 The rule: "Never hardcode secrets, API keys, passwords, or tokens in source code."
 The rule: "Always create a checkpoint before making large structural changes."

Step 3 — Tool Schemas: Pass all 18 tool schemas from AgentToolRegistry.TOOL_SCHEMAS to every Bedrock API call.

Step 4 — Agent Loop: Enter a loop that runs for at most config.MAX_AGENT_LOOP_ITERATIONS iterations or until the elapsed time exceeds config.MAX_AGENT_SESSION_MINUTES * 60 seconds.

On each iteration:
1. Check context token count via BedrockClaudeClient.count_tokens_approx(messages). If > config.MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS * 0.95, trigger context compression: summarize the oldest 50% of the conversation into a single assistant message ("Summary of prior work: ..."), replace those messages with the summary, and log a context_compressed event.
2. Load the last N tool results from Dragonfly dtg:{session_id}:trajectory. Run DTGClassifier.classify(...). If any instructions were returned, format them via DTGClassifier.format_for_injection(...) and append to the last message in the messages array (inplace modification, not a new message).
3. Check for doom loop escalation: If the returned instructions contain doom_loop_escalate, call async def _invoke_consultant(self, session_id, project_id, ws_send) (described below), inject the consultant's plan into the messages as an assistant message preceded by "[CONSULTANT AGENT PLAN]:", reset the doom counter, and continue the loop.
4. Call BedrockClaudeClient.converse_stream(messages, system_prompt, tools). For each yielded event:
    If type == "text_delta": append text to the current assistant turn buffer, send {"type": "agent_text_delta", "payload": {"text": chunk.text}} via ws_send.
    If type == "tool_use": collect the complete tool use block. Send {"type": "tool_start", "payload": {"tool_name": name, "tool_use_id": id, "tool_input": input}} via ws_send. Execute the tool via AgentToolRegistry.execute_tool(...). Send {"type": "tool_result", "payload": {"tool_name": name, "tool_use_id": id, "content": result.content, "is_error": result.is_error, "execution_time_ms": result.execution_time_ms}} via ws_send. Append the tool result to Dragonfly dtg:{session_id}:trajectory (JSONserialized, LTRIM to last DTG_TRAJECTORY_WINDOW items). Update doom_counter in agent state if a doomlooprelevant pattern was just recorded.
    If type == "stop" with stop_reason == "end_turn": the model has finished generating without a tool call. Append the complete assistant message to conversation history. Save history to Dragonfly. Set agent status to "idle". Send {"type": "agent_done", "payload": {"message": accumulated_text}} via ws_send. Return.
    If type == "stop" with stop_reason == "tool_use": the model has requested tool execution. After all tool calls in this batch are executed, append both the assistant message (with its tool use blocks) and all tool result messages to the conversation history. Save to Dragonfly. Update agent state (increment loop_count). Continue to the next iteration.
5. Update agent state in Dragonfly at the end of each iteration: increment loop_count, update last_active, update context_token_count.

Step 5 — Doom Loop Consultant Invocation: Implement async def _invoke_consultant(self, session_id, project_id, ws_send). This method:
1. Sends {"type": "agent_status", "payload": {"status": "consulting", "message": "Doom loop detected. Consulting secondary model for fresh perspective..."}} via ws_send.
2. Reads the last 10 tool results from the trajectory in Dragonfly.
3. Reads the last 5 messages from the conversation history.
4. Reads the current versions of all files that were edited in the last 10 loop iterations (identified from write_file tool calls in the trajectory).
5. Constructs a problem_summary string and a context_snippet string from the above data.
6. Calls GLM5Client.consult(problem_summary, context_snippet).
7. Returns the consultant's plan string.
8. Sends {"type": "agent_status", "payload": {"status": "running", "message": "Consultant plan received. Resuming..."}} via ws_send.

Step 6 — Plan Mode Handling: If mode == "plan", the system prompt addition says: "You are in Plan Mode. Do NOT write any files or execute any commands. Your only output should be a numbered task list describing exactly what you will build and how. After completing the plan, ask the user to confirm before proceeding." In Plan Mode, the agent loop runs exactly one iteration (since the model should output text only, not call tools) and returns after producing the plan text.

Step 7 — Max Autonomy Mode Handling: If mode == "max_autonomy", remove all confirmationrequesting language from the system prompt. Increase config.MAX_AGENT_LOOP_ITERATIONS to 200 for this session only. After every 20 iterations, automatically call create_checkpoint tool with the description "Auto-checkpoint at iteration {loop_count}".

3. Stores the PTY process in an instance dict keyed by session_id.

async def write_input(self, session_id: str, data: str) — writes data to the PTY stdin. data may be any terminal input including control characters.

async def read_output_loop(self, session_id: str, ws_send: Callable) — runs in a background asyncio task, continuously reads from the PTY using asyncio.get_event_loop().run_in_executor(None, pty.read, 1024), and sends each chunk to the client via ws_send with message {"type": "terminal_output", "payload": {"data": chunk_str}}. Handles EOFError from the PTY when the shell exits.

async def close_session(self, session_id: str) — terminates the PTY process.

 III.18 — WebSocket Handler

Implement a single FastAPI WebSocket endpoint at /ws/{project_id} that handles all realtime communication for a project session.

The WebSocket handler must:
1. Accept the connection and immediately validate the JWT from the query parameter ?token=.
2. On authentication failure, send {"type": "error", "payload": {"code": "AUTH_FAILED", "message": "Invalid or expired token"}} and close the connection with code 4001.
3. On success, send {"type": "connected", "payload": {"session_id": str, "project_id": str, "user": {"username": str, "user_id": str}}}.
4. Create a terminal session via TerminalManager.create_session.
5. Start the terminal output read loop as a background task.
6. Start a log stream background task: subscribe to the Dragonfly pub/sub channel run:{project_id}:log_stream, and for each published message forward it to the client as {"type": "log_line", "payload": {"line": str}}.
7. Enter a loop receiving messages from the WebSocket client. Parse each message as a WebSocketMessage. Handle the following message types:
    "terminal_input": calls TerminalManager.write_input(session_id, payload["data"]).
    "agent_chat": validates the payload["message"] and payload["mode"] fields; creates an AgentChatRequest; if an agent loop is already running for this session, sends {"type": "error", "payload": {"message": "Agent is already running"}} and ignores the request; otherwise launches AgentLoop.run(...) as a background task with ws_send bound to the current WebSocket's send_json method.
    "agent_stop": sets the agent session status to "stopping" in Dragonfly, which causes the agent loop to exit after the current tool call completes.
    "file_save": calls ProjectManager.write_file(project_id, payload["path"], payload["content"]), then sends {"type": "file_saved", "payload": {"path": str}}.
    "run_project": calls ProcessRunner.start(project_id, payload.get("command") or project_meta.run_command, project_meta.port).
    "stop_project": calls ProcessRunner.stop(project_id).
    "create_snapshot": calls SnapshotEngine.create_snapshot(...) and sends the result as {"type": "snapshot_created", "payload": snapshot.dict()}.
    "restore_snapshot": calls SnapshotEngine.restore_snapshot(...) and sends {"type": "snapshot_restored", "payload": {"snapshot_id": str}}.
    "install_package": calls NixEnvironmentManager.install_package(...) for each package, sends progress updates.
    "ping": sends {"type": "pong", "payload": {"timestamp": float}}.
8. On WebSocket disconnect (clean or unclean), cancel all background tasks (terminal read loop, log stream loop, any running agent loop), close the PTY session, and clean up session state.

The handler uses an asyncio.Queue to coordinate background tasks with the main receive loop, and asyncio.wait_for with appropriate timeouts on all blocking operations.

Implementálj egy NixEnvironmentManager osztályt, amely a projekt Nix‑alapú fejlesztői környezetét kezeli.

Az env.nix formátum:

A cache fájl .cache/env.json formátuma:

json
{
  "env_nix_hash": "<sha256 of env.nix content>",
  "evaluated_at": "<ISO timestamp>",
  "env_vars": {
    "PATH": "/nix/store/...-python3-3.12.x/bin:/nix/store/...:...",
    "NIX_CC": "/nix/store/...",
    "PKG_CONFIG_PATH": "...",
    ...
  },
  "store_paths": [
    "/nix/store/abc123-python3-3.12.x",
    "/nix/store/def456-gcc-13.2.0",
    ...
  ]
